author: netrunnereve
body:
Have you tried using a non MOE model? From my experience split mode works pretty well with RADV and it's only a bit slower than running on one card. 

Also yeah you should be only using split mode layer with Vulkan, not row.

author: hjc4869
body: I have the exact same GPU setup locally, and found that the GPU frequency were significantly lower when using Vulkan comparing to ROCm (both running `-sm layer`). It's usually running at 1.3 GHz on Vulkan and 2.0 GHz on ROCm. The GPU could be more sensitive to power savings when running Vulkan and not fully loaded.

author: netrunnereve
body:
Interesting. I guess the next thing to try is to lock the graphics clock to see if you get better performance there, if that's the issue then it's probably a driver bug.

If not then it [might be a GTT issue](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/13765) and you can try with `RADV_PERFTEST=nogttspill` if your Mesa if new enough. Other than that I'm out of ideas.

On my AMD cards with RADV I basically get full graphics and memory clock speeds if I use one or two GPUs and it doesn't slow down like this.

author: hjc4869
body: The clock behavior is more like an AMD driver/firmware thing rather than anything to do with llama.cpp. It's possible to lock the frequency with `sudo rocm-smi --setperflevel high`, but on W7900 the max clock available in this way is only around 1.7 GHz so still not the best possible setup. Ideally we need to find a way to let the GPU prefer lower latency in light load.

author: netrunnereve
body:
> Row and Layer performance does increase but None performance decreases, not to mention the idle power draw increases to 70W instead of 10W

Well your numbers look right if that your card does 2 GHz on none in auto mode and 1.7 GHz with it set to high. Unfortunately like @hjc4869 said this is a driver issue and there's nothing we can do about it in llama.cpp. If you want to dig deeper you can try [making a custom power profile](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/626464/how-do-i-use-the-custom-powerplay-power-profile-in-amdgpu) in amdgpu to make it increase the clock even when the card isn't doing a lot of work.

author: IMbackK
body:
> The clock behavior is more like an AMD driver/firmware thing rather than anything to do with llama.cpp. It's possible to lock the frequency with `sudo rocm-smi --setperflevel high`, but on W7900 the max clock available in this way is only around 1.7 GHz so still not the best possible setup. Ideally we need to find a way to let the GPU prefer lower latency in light load.

The VR power profile provides this, that is its purpose, since VR is exteamly latency sensitive. For vr, not compute, i did write a small utility that runs a command with the VR power profile active and returns to the default profile on exit: https://uvos.xyz/git/uvos/vrmode note that its specific to my machine, you will have to change the gpu id(s) and the program assumes you have at least two numa nodes

body: rocm-smi doesn't seem to reset previous settings without a clean reboot, I only got 1.6 GHz before that. Did a clean boot and added the following command to the systemd service, now the two GPUs are running at ~2 GHz. ExecStartPre=bash -c '/usr/bin/rocm-smi --setprofile 5 -d 1 && /usr/bin/rocm-smi --setprofile 5 -d 2' Even at 2 GHz it's still a little lower than running the model on a single GPU (>2.7 GHz), though that's already lots of perf uplift comparing to default settings.
